reasoning: Patient is alert and oriented with stable vital signs (all within normal limits).
Chief complaint is a retained foreign body in rectum — requires procedural intervention but not immediately life-threatening.
Absence of abdominal pain/tenderness is reassuring against perforation, peritonitis, or acute obstruction.

At triage, no evidence of high-risk vital sign abnormalities or shock.

Patient will require multiple resources: physician evaluation, likely imaging (CT or plain films to locate object), possible procedural removal (rigid/flexible endoscopy ± manual extraction), and potential surgical standby if complications arise.
Two or more resources anticipated → meets ESI-3 threshold.
Red flag to monitor: perforation risk increases with time; retained sharp or caustic objects pose higher risk. However, 12-hour duration without pain/peritoneal signs is lower-risk presentation.
No prior record limits historical context but does not change acute assessment.

Confidence tempered by: (1) unknown object composition/size/acuity of insertion; (2) single snapshot assessment; (3) potential for delayed presentation of complications (perforation can be subtle early).
red_flags: Retained foreign body — risk of perforation, sepsis, or hemorrhage if object is sharp, caustic, or causes obstruction.
Absence of pain may be falsely reassuring; perforation can present insidiously in young, otherwise healthy patients.
No prior history — cannot assess baseline abdominal exam or prior similar incidents.
If vitals deteriorate, abdominal tenderness develops, or signs of peritonitis/sepsis emerge → escalate immediately to ESI-2.
